title: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors
description: Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere.Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in
body: Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere.Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in popularity in 2021 alongside the cryptocurrency boom, becoming status symbols for celebrities and wealthy collectors.Weekly NFT trading volume across major blockchains surged from about $4.4 million in late 2020 to a peak of $3.2 billion in August 2021, according to CryptoSlam data published by The Block.Today, much of that trading activity has disappeared. Weekly NFT trading volume has fallen more than 99% since August 2021, and several major NFT marketplaces have closed. On Thursday, Blur, once the largest marketplace for Ethereum-based NFTs, shut down its website.At the height of the boom, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey sold an NFT of his first tweet for $2.9 million, while a digital artwork by an artist known as Beeple fetched $69.3 million at Christie's. Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon showed off their Bored Ape NFTs on "The Tonight Show," and even McDonald's released NFTs celebrating the return of its McRib sandwich.Back then, some buyers believed NFTs represented the future of digital ownership, while others bet they could resell them at higher prices. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the demand that had driven the digital tokens' values higher.The NFT boom and bust shows how quickly speculative investments can unravel when demand dries up. For investors, it's a cautionary tale about spotting the warning signs before buying into the next craze, financial experts tell CNBC Make It.Why did NFTs collapse?Part of the initial appeal of NFTs was the promise of a new way for artists and other creators to make money from their work. Using blockchain technology, NFTs allowed creators to sell digital collectibles with verifiable ownership records and potentially earn royalties on subsequent sales through smart contracts.More broadly, NFTs were touted as part of the future of digital ownership, with the potential to transform how people bought, sold and traded digital assets.But establishing ownership of a digital collectible was different from creating lasting demand for it, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at wealth management firm Scholar Advising. "NFTs tried to manufacture that demand," he says. "Blockchain could establish who owns the token, but it couldn't guarantee that anyone would really value the ownership at the end of the day."In practice, many of the NFTs that attracted attention were relatively simple digital images, such as cartoon animals or promotional artwork featuring beer cans.Traditional collectibles, such as paintings, antiques and baseball cards, have established histories and communities of collectors that can sustain demand, Mills says. NFTs, by comparison, became enormously popular in a relatively short period.Unlike many traditional collectibles, however, NFTs could be created in virtually unlimited quantities. While individual collections might contain a limited number of tokens, there was little stopping creators from launching new series. At the height of the boom in 2022, roughly 500 new NFT collections were being created every day, according to blockchain analytics firm IntoTheBlock.The rapid rise in NFT prices helped fuel expectations that buyers would continue paying more for them. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the pool of potential buyers.And unlike stocks or bonds, most NFTs didn't generate income, meaning buyers hoping to turn a profit generally depended on someone else being willing to pay more for them, says Martin Mulyadi, the YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting at Shenandoah University."Most NFTs paid nothing, so the only way to make money was finding a next buyer at a higher price," he says. "When the buyers stopped coming, there was nothing holding up the price." What everyday investors can learnFor everyday investors, the NFT bust is a reminder that an asset's popularity doesn't necessarily make it a worthwhile investment.One common justification for buying risky investments like collectibles is that they make up only a small portion of an otherwise diversified portfolio. Financial advisors often recommend limiting speculative holdings to money an investor can afford to lose. But keeping an investment small doesn't necessarily make it worthwhile, Mulyadi says."While keeping a bet small limits the damage, it doesn't turn a weak asset into a good one," he says.Mills argues that investors can also confuse speculation with diversification."Diversification is not just owning more things," he says. "It's owning things that have different economic characteristics that change the risk and return of your overall portfolio."For collectibles, that means looking beyond an item's scarcity or popularity to whether there's an established market of buyers likely to value it over time. Even then, future demand can be difficult to predict. There's also a difference between buying a collectible because you actually like it and buying it because you think someone else will pay more for it. For many NFT speculators, the appeal was likely less about owning what was essentially a JPEG than the prospect of reselling it for a profit.Before buying a speculative asset, Mills recommends asking two questions: What is the economic reason it should generate a return, and what role does it play in the overall portfolio? If an investor can't answer those questions, he says, the investment may not belong in the portfolio at all."A bad investment doesn't become a good investment just because you only own a little bit of it," Mills says.

schema.headline: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors

title: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first
description: SpaceX Starship 42 returns from orbit to the launch pad on the 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, on Nov. 14, 2026.Jo
body: SpaceX Starship 42 returns from orbit to the launch pad on the 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, on Nov. 14, 2026.Joe Skipper | ReutersAfter a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company.SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas.Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage. Musk posted a video on X inspecting the upper stage craft after completing the capture.During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water. The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla.The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.)Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA. Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary." During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network.The company's constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

schema.headline: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first

title: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%
description: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesOdds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 climbed to 62% from 27% since Thursday on Kalshi.Chances that tha
body: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesOdds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 climbed to 62% from 27% since Thursday on Kalshi.Chances that that Elon Musk's two companies, SpaceX, a satellite and rocket maker, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, will soon integrate have jumped across multiple Kalshi markets since late last week. The contract asks "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and would be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. On Friday, Walter Isaacson, a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" he's confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a catalyst."I think you have to have a merger. Makes no sense otherwise," Isaacson said. Tesla's 2026 annual shareholder meeting, set for Dec. 3, may provide more insight into a potential linkup, Isaacson said. While speculators are anticipating an announcement of a merger this year, a research note from Jefferies last week said a deal will likely face backlash after the Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships in the midterm elections earlier this month. "We understand there is higher risk of scrutiny post elections, but the vision of a combined SpaceX and Tesla as proxies for longer-term U.S. national strategies of independence and leadership in space, energy, manufacturing or semiconductors, in our view, remain highly relevant regardless of which party controls Congress," wrote Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois. Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, said a possible merger between Musk's two companies would face "tremendous scrutiny," Bloomberg reported Thursday. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%

title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
description: Actor Robert Pattinson at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 5th, 2026. Laurent Koffel | Gamma-rapho | Getty ImagesRobert Pattinson has been cast
body: Actor Robert Pattinson at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 5th, 2026. Laurent Koffel | Gamma-rapho | Getty ImagesRobert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic. The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin," Villeneuve said.In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond

title: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
description: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday h
body: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road.""I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy. In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint.""After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

schema.headline: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’

title: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly
description: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesBitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weak
body: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesBitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower. On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBitcoin just logged its sixth consecutive week of declinesBitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets.On Friday, the dollar index – which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin – reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen."A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia's results add to the tech selling," he said. "The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over."Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, said he's monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides."Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling," he said. "For a recovery to hold, spot buyers need to keep showing up after the forced selling has passed."

schema.headline: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly

title: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial
description: A Wegovy injection pen arranged in Waterbury, Vermont, US, on Monday, April 28, 2025. Shelby Knowles | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNovo on Monday released
body: A Wegovy injection pen arranged in Waterbury, Vermont, US, on Monday, April 28, 2025. Shelby Knowles | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNovo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial. When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications."This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity. In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040. While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6. In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September. "We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids. Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said. "That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

schema.headline: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

title: U.S. crude oil declines to $87 a barrel on recovering Middle East exports
description: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Ira
body: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.Eli Hartman | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesOil prices are falling Monday as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover and tensions between Iran and the U.S remain at a stalemate.Brent crude fell 2% to $93.90 per barrel Monday while West Texas Intermediate crude slipped 1.8% to about $87 per barrel. The International Energy Agency said on Friday it expects global supply to exceed 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter of 2026, reversing its earlier forecast for a deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global demand and even as shipping attacks continue.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconWTI Crude, YTDMeanwhile, Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, according to the International Energy Agency.Goldman Sachs said in a Sunday note it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to a surplus. The bank believes idle East supply to rise above its 2025 average as producers use ship-to-ship transfers and add pipeline capacity.

schema.headline: U.S. crude oil declines to $87 a barrel on recovering Middle East exports

title: International student enrollment drops sharply, putting more U.S. colleges in financial jeopardy
description: Students walk around the UCLA campus, in Los Angeles, Oct. 7, 2025.Juliana Yamada | Los Angeles Times | Getty ImagesAmid changing visa policies and ri
body: Students walk around the UCLA campus, in Los Angeles, Oct. 7, 2025.Juliana Yamada | Los Angeles Times | Getty ImagesAmid changing visa policies and rising degree costs, significantly fewer new international students enrolled at U.S. colleges this year — a shift that could have financial repercussions for colleges, students and the broader economy.In the fall 2026 semester, the tally of new international students studying in the U.S. fell 15% compared with the prior academic year, according to a fall snapshot released Monday by the nonprofit Institute of International Education.Over the 2025-26 academic year, the number of new international students in the U.S. fell more than 17%, largely because fewer graduate students came from countries such as India and China, the IIE's report found.A growing number of U.S. colleges said international student recruitment was a top concern, but the report also cited as significant barriers the high cost of a U.S. degree relative to other countries and uncertainty around new rules ending the traditional "duration of status" system and limiting most F-1 and J-1 visas to four years.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings capWhy Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investorsSocial Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARPCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Even though the Department of Homeland Security's new visa restrictions are currently on hold under a federal court injunction, experts say questions about the changing policies may have already discouraged some prospective international students."At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the United States should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it," Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a Sept. 14 statement after a federal court temporarily blocked the Department of Homeland Security's new visa rules.Foreign students typically pay full tuition, making international enrollment an important revenue source for colleges and universities, according to Robert Franek, editor-in-chief of The Princeton Review.With fewer tuition dollars coming in, there are fewer resources for U.S. students, particularly for financial aid, he said: "There are going to be fewer research dollars, fewer scholarship dollars for students here in the states." The economic falloutInternational students also contributed nearly $40 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2025-26 academic year, according to a NAFSA analysis. This year's enrollment decline is expected to cost the economy roughly $2.4 billion."The data again reflect the harsh reality that the barriers the U.S. government is putting in place to block talented international students are having a real impact," NAFSA's Aw said. "All Americans will feel the effects as international students' tuition payments, local spending, and contributions to U.S. excellence in research and innovation diminish."Although the fallout extends well beyond college campuses, other research shows that colleges and the students they serve will bear the brunt of the impact.An analysis by Fitch Ratings released in August said recent changes to F-1 student visa rules could heighten financial risks for some U.S. colleges and universities, particularly those that rely heavily on students from abroad."Sustained drops in new international student enrollment can have outsized revenue effects, as international students often pay full tuition or receive less institutional aid than domestic students," Fitch analysts said in the report. "Lost revenue is hard to replace quickly."Specifically, universities with large graduate and STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — programs, in which time to degree completion can exceed four years, will have a harder time sustaining the enrollment pipeline and "may incur higher costs to address overseas recruitment challenges," the analysts wrote. Most international students — 57% — study in STEM fields, according to IIE's report, so enrollment declines can have an outsized financial impact on schools with large engineering and computer science programs.Underscoring the importance of those students, 91% of colleges and universities said recruiting international students in STEM fields is now a key priority, according to IIE's fall snapshot, which was based on a survey of 809 institutions.Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: International student enrollment drops sharply, putting more U.S. colleges in financial jeopardy

title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
description: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annu
body: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.  Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion. "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message. The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the artificial intelligence buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk. The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points. In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year. Confidence in BerkshireBuffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel: "My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity. ... You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said.Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.""Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter.Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

schema.headline: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter

title: NATO member Estonia to close Russia border after attempted 'sabotage' of drone maker
description: A woman walks to Russia from Estonia at the Luhamaa border crossing on October 3, 2025 in Luhamaa, Estonia.Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty Imag
body: A woman walks to Russia from Estonia at the Luhamaa border crossing on October 3, 2025 in Luhamaa, Estonia.Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesNATO member Estonia says it is preparing to close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies.Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that Russia's military intelligence service GRU had ordered an arson attack against Estonian drone maker Threod Systems in the early hours of Saturday morning.Authorities said the attempted attack did not cause significant damage and eight people were detained in connection with it.Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, said closing the crossings would help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.Tallinn has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Ukraine since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.  "This weekend's attempted sabotage against an Estonian defence company, attributed by our security authorities to Russia's GRU, is yet another reminder that Russia's hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Sunday via social media."Estonia is preparing to close its road border crossings with Russia in response. Hostile actions must have consequences." A coat of arms of the Estonian police and the Estonian flag are displayed on the uniform of an Estonian policeman standing on the border bridge from the Estonian city of Narva to Russia.Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesTsahkna said he had informed his Finnish, Lithuanian and Latvian counterparts of the decision.Russia's foreign ministry said it would assess Estonia's plans to close its border crossings, adding that if these plans were to come into force, it would be seen as "yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," according to state news agency Tass.It did not directly comment on the accusation that Moscow is responsible for the attack on Threod Systems."Estonia is building walls. Many countries, as history shows, have built walls that have brought no good to their creators," Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov said Monday, according to comments reported by Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.Estonia PM: 'We will not be intimidated'Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack was part of Russia's broader "hybrid war" against Europe."We will not be intimidated. Estonia is preparing for the possibility of closing its border with Russia to reduce the risks to our people and national security," Michal said Sunday via social media.  The latest incident follows an arson attack in mid-August against Milrem Robotics, an Estonian defense company that supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles. Estonian authorities later blamed Russia for the attack. Moscow denied the allegation.European security officials and lawmakers have previously warned about Russia's hybrid warfare. In September, Danish intelligence officials said Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.

schema.headline: NATO member Estonia to close Russia border after attempted 'sabotage' of drone maker

title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
description: Sankaet Pathak, CEO and founder of Foundation, a company that builds a humanoid robot Phantom-01, poses for a photo during an interview with Reuters a
body: Sankaet Pathak, CEO and founder of Foundation, a company that builds a humanoid robot Phantom-01, poses for a photo during an interview with Reuters at his company's factory in San Francisco, California, U.S., February 4, 2026. Aleksandra Michalska | ReutersFoundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts. "What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.'Plain sight'That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business."We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands."Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism."Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."Phantom-01, a humanoid robot developed by San Francisco-based startup Foundation for military purposes, sits at the company's factory in San Francisco, California, U.S., February 4, 2026. Aleksandra Michalska | ReutersEric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal. In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.Rescue loan?Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said."This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages. The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.Missing moneyBefore Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks. Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula. Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview."I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

schema.headline: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home

title: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
description: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025
body: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025.Annabelle Gordon | ReutersSen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaTrump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends LutnickNvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictionsNvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exitThe tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growingNvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignationMegaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probeAlice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls."The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act, which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons, who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology.""America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December.Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

schema.headline: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
description: Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning i
body: Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report."Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.watch nowMegaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.The company, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation.""Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.The company added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.

schema.headline: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business

title: ‘Standing on one leg’: IMF chief warns about global economy as AI circular financing hits $1 trillion
description: Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), during the 2026 Michel Camdessus Central Banking Lecture at the IMF
body: Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), during the 2026 Michel Camdessus Central Banking Lecture at the IMF headquarters in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe global economy is "on the AI leg," International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday, warning that the overdependence on the sector risks the world's financial stability. Georgieva flagged that a "sudden drop in investment confidence and withdrawal from the AI field" could weaken economic growth, speaking with CNBC's JP Ong on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' summit in the Philippines."We have a world economy that is standing on one leg on the AI leg. If this leg wobbles, that can lead to financial stability troubles," Georgieva warned. Circular financing among AI companies — where money invested in an AI company ultimately flows back to the investor through purchase orders — has grown to a little over $1 trillion, two-thirds of it funded by debt, the IMF estimates. "It's not a huge size, but it is a rapid increase," Georgieva said.Nvidia Corp, which has seen more than $1 trillion wiped out of its market value over the past month, is at the center of these circular financial deals. The fallout from the chipmaker's former CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has led to a sell-off in global AI-linked stocks and put the spotlight on the company's role as a key financier of the AI infrastructure buildout. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated in a recent note that an Nvidia financing pullback could easily remove $50 billion or more out of the system, at a time when rising interest rates have already made corporate borrowing more expensive.  Economy vulnerable to AI bustGeorgieva's warning comes as the AI build-out has been a critical engine of growth for the global economy, propping up trade and investment. The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% in October as major economies lean on AI investment to power growth otherwise curtailed by the energy crunch caused by the Iran war.   The institution estimated that about 40% of the world's workforce will be affected by AI. Capital Economics suggested that as much as 80% of the recent expansion in global exports was concentrated in AI-related goods. watch nowInvestors' frenzy for AI reflects expectations running ahead of what the technology has proven to deliver, Georgieva said. "We tend to rush ahead," as valuations climb, she said, therefore "some corrections" become necessary. IMF in October had warned that a short-term disappointment could set off a disorderly correction across asset classes: in its worst case scenario, if AI fails to live up to the market's lofty expectations, U.S. equity prices could fall 20% in 2026 and global output end up 1.1% below its baseline estimate by 2028. Global equites, including U.S. chipmakers, have been seeing a bruising sell-off over the past few weeks, with investor appetite for the AI trade facing a fresh test this week ahead of earnings from Nvidia and Anthropic's blockbuster listing. Georgieva on Monday characterized the recent market swings as "orderly," and unlikely to spiral into anything that could undermine the world economy, while urging caution. "We have to be watchful."

schema.headline: ‘Standing on one leg’: IMF chief warns about global economy as AI circular financing hits $1 trillion
